archive.title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
archive.summary: CorrespondentReporting fromTirana, Albania Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row. Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests. The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time. Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.
archive.editorialText: CorrespondentReporting fromTirana, Albania Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row. Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests. The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time. Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration. Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street. The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday. During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.

archive.title: India’s Cockroach Janta party leader arrested amid crackdown on protests
archive.summary: The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday and then later formally arrested as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital. Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag. On Saturday local media reported he was arrested “to prevent a breach of the peace”, with broadcasters NDTV and India Today saying he would be called before a special executive ⁠magistrate later in the day.

archive.title: Global survey links financial hardship to lower trust in science
archive.summary: Poor access to health care, limited local influence over research priorities and an unequal distribution of scientific benefits are undermining public confidence in science, experts warn, following the release of a global trust survey. The Wellcome Global Monitor 2026 surveyed more than 140,000 people in 140 countries in 2025 and found that trust in science had fallen below prepandemic levels. To track changes over time, researchers compared results from 108 countries surveyed in 2018, 2020 and 2025.
archive.editorialText: Poor access to health care, limited local influence over research priorities and an unequal distribution of scientific benefits are undermining public confidence in science, experts warn, following the release of a global trust survey. The Wellcome Global Monitor 2026 surveyed more than 140,000 people in 140 countries in 2025 and found that trust in science had fallen below prepandemic levels. To track changes over time, researchers compared results from 108 countries surveyed in 2018, 2020 and 2025. The proportion of respondents expressing at least some trust in science fell from 77% in 2018 to 72% in 2025, after rising to 80% during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Over the same period, the share reporting little or no trust in science rose from 13% in both 2018 and 2020 to 19% in 2025. Trust in scientists themselves also declined. The share of people expressing "a lot" of trust in scientists dropped to 32% in 2025, down from 34% in 2018 and 43% in 2020. archive.summary: Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. Just ahead of the wider release of Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, TikTok has banned the film’s social media account from its platform. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, was informed Friday afternoon that a “permanent suspension” was imminent. Bleecker Street has not yet responded to a request for comment from The Verge. While TikTok has no official affiliation with Elon Musk, part owner Larry Ellison appears in the film via a text message offering to help Musk fund his Twitter purchase.

archive.title: France protests: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as over 1,000 arrested
archive.summary: Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living. At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets. In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds. Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse. Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported.

archive.summary: It's well known that alcohol has profound consequences on the way the brain works, and research shows that even low levels of the drug can damage your brain. But how does alcohol actually cause brain damage at the cellular level? In a surprising discovery reported in Immunity, scientists found that alcohol doesn't just interact with neurons. archive.editorialText: It's well known that alcohol has profound consequences on the way the brain works, and research shows that even low levels of the drug can damage your brain. But how does alcohol actually cause brain damage at the cellular level? In a surprising discovery reported in Immunity, scientists found that alcohol doesn't just interact with neurons. New findings show the drug also affects immune cells in the brain called microglia, triggering them to dismantle the extracellular matrix that structurally supports brain cells. "For years, alcohol's effects on the brain were largely viewed through the lens of neurons, and for good reason: alcohol acts directly on neuronal receptors," says neuroscientist and senior author of the study Dimitrios Davalos from the Cleveland Clinic. "By following microglia in real time, we were able to see that they aren't simply responding to damage. They drive the detrimental changes alcohol causes in the brain." Microglia are specialized immune cells that continually monitor and maintain the brain by detecting threats, clearing out dead cells and damaged tissue, and pruning neuronal connections. Here, and perhaps even earlier, lie the foundations of extensive trade routes as we know them today. Associate professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University, Antalya, has worked along this coastline for decades excavating ancient shipwrecks. Acting on clues from local seafarers, Öniz found a shipwreck in shallow waters off Kekova, west of Antalya in Turkey, in 2024. Earlier this year, he contacted me and asked if I would help date some of the pottery vessels found on this wreck. As an archaeologist specializing in desert sites, I found this a singular experience.
archive.editorialText: A shipwreck off the coast of Turkey is the oldest shipwreck in the world, our team of archaeologists believes. There's little left of the ship itself, but based on clues from its cargo—including pottery vessels—a research team I was part of has tentatively dated the wreck to around 2700–2400 B.C. That's about 4,500 years ago. Prior to this discovery, the world's oldest shipwreck was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, in Greece, thought to have been from about 4,200 years ago. Much work remains to be done to finesse the conclusions, and a paper outlining the results is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal. Yet the discovery could transform our understanding of ancient Mediterranean connections during the Early Bronze Age. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own.

archive.title: 2,200-Year-Old Fingerprints Reveal Who Really Built China's Mysterious Terracotta Army
archive.summary: Traditionally, archaeologists have assumed that the entire army was built by adult men. New research reveals that this assumption may be wrong. The sculptors – whose work endures long after the emperor they served – left their fingerprints in the still-wet clay, and it's those fingerprints that suggest men, women, and children likely all collaborated in the epic undertaking of the Terracotta Army. "These findings challenge the long-held assumption that Terracotta Army production relied exclusively on adult male labor," write researchers led by archaeologist Xiaoxi Li of Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum, "providing the first quantitative biological evidence for a diverse workforce including women and children."

Haojing Yan, a professor of physics and astronomy in Mizzou's College of Arts and Science, heads the international team behind the Roman eXtreme Deep Field (RXDF), a project that will use NASA's newest flagship space observatory, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, to create one of the deepest and widest views of the early universe ever made. The study is published on the arXiv preprint server. And NASA is giving Yan and the team 386 hours of observation time to do it. archive.summary: SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korea said Saturday it had successfully tested a new torpedo system that uses artificial intelligence for target detection and guidance. The Korean Central News Agency said the weapon tested Thursday was a “super-speed, precisely guided” torpedo system named Zam-2.0. It didn’t explain what was meant by artificial intelligence. The report added that test verified the weapon’s propulsion systems, which were developed through more than 180 tests over the past five years. South Korea’s military, which often accuses the North of exaggerating its military technologies, did not immediately comment on KCNA’s report.

archive.title: Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California
archive.summary: Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California. The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River.

archive.title: Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
archive.summary: A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public. The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand Condé" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the Château de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple. The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.

archive.summary: Also on Friday, the Pope phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin from hospital to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where access to food and water has been cut off for thousands. "The fact that he accepted the call and spoke with the Pope may, I hope, be a sign that the Pope's request will indeed be carried out," said Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state. Without mentioning a ceasefire, the Kremlin said: "The Vatican's intention to help create the conditions necessary to ensure the safety of the town's population and to organise vital supplies has been supported".

archive.title: Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable
archive.summary: As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian. Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.

archive.title: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
archive.summary: Scientists at the University of Southern California (USC) have discovered a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of cancer-fighting immune cells, opening a promising new direction for cancer treatment. By working with immature cells that can develop into powerful immune defenders, the researchers have created a system capable of generating large numbers of genetically engineered cells that recognize tumors and help activate the body's natural defenses. The breakthrough, described in a study published in Cell, could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles facing cancer immunotherapy, including the difficulty of manufacturing enough immune cells and keeping them active in the body.
archive.displayTitle: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
archive.originalSummary: USC scientists have discovered a way to create a potentially renewable supply of genetically engineered immune cells that can attack cancer and strengthen the body's natural defenses. By growing and modifying immature immune cells rather than mature ones, researchers developed a system that can continuously produce tumor-fighting cells inside the body.

archive.title: A highway instead of a racetrack: Strong coupling of light and sound in an optical fiber
archive.summary: For the first time, scientists have achieved strong coupling between light and long-lived acoustic vibrations in an optical fiber. Optical fibers are used in both classical telecommunications and quantum communication and could serve not only as connections between computing nodes but also as quantum processors themselves in the future. The results, published in Nature Physics, pave the way for new technologies in quantum signal processing. Mechanical and acoustic vibrations can be used to convert signals across various frequency ranges, from optical frequencies (terahertz) to microwaves (gigahertz) and even lower frequencies (megahertz or kilohertz). For instance, this capability is essential to connect multiple quantum computers operating at gigahertz frequencies via optical links.

archive.title: Mysterious 'Golden Tree' Coral Is So Weird, Scientists Had to Create a New Family on The Tree of Life
archive.summary: The newly discovered coral lives in strange conditions that seem inhospitable to life. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute/Breedy et al., ZooKeys, 2026) In the twilight deeps of the Eastern Pacific Ocean, a magical sight can be found on a seamount off the coast of Costa Rica. As the underwater vehicle SuBastian glides over a rocky outcrop oddly coated with a fuzzy pink patina and punctuated with basket-shaped gleaming white sponges, a majestic yellow form emerges from the darkness. It looks like a golden tree, so vividly yellow you can imagine it glowing. Then, as the camera zooms closer, you can see the pink fuzz moving – a thick carpet of stars from which the golden tree blooms.

archive.title: Google's Quantum Computer Just Achieved a Major Breakthrough With 'Magic States'
archive.summary: Quantum computers have an inconvenient problem: they're magnificently efficient at making mistakes. These marvelous machines could one day solve problems that would bring even the most powerful conventional supercomputers to their knees. But the quantum states behind their incredible computing power are also exceptionally fragile, and keeping errors under control is a monumental task. In fact, a fully functional quantum computer could end up devoting most of its resources not to performing calculations, but simply to making sure those calculations are correct. Now, the wizards at Google have demonstrated a new way to make quantum computing significantly less error-prone, using a technique with the delightfully appropriate name "magic state cultivation".

archive.title: Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’
archive.summary: Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries ⁠after Zelenskyy said Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire unilaterally declared by Trump on Sunday, having briefly halted its attacks to demonstrate its readiness for peace talks. Russia had continued its strikes on Ukrainian power plants. In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, the US president said: “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace.

archive.title: Norman McCubbin obituary
archive.summary: My brother Norman McCubbin, who has died aged 77, was a scientist who worked at the forefront of experimental particle physics. A leading light in experiments that took place on the Large Hadron Collider, the world’s biggest and most powerful particle accelerator at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (Cern) in Switzerland, he spent the last five years of his working life as director of the particle physics department at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) in Oxfordshire, until his retirement in 2012. Afterwards he became a tutor to undergraduates at St Anne’s College, Oxford, and was still in that role at his death.
